nameStory: Euastrum humerosum doesn't have a widely-used common name, as this tiny freshwater algae is mainly known to scientists and microscopy enthusiasts. The scientific name Euastrum comes from Greek words meaning 'beautiful star,' referring to its symmetrical, star-like shape when viewed under a microscope. The species name 'humerosum' means 'having shoulders,' describing the distinctive shoulder-like projections on each half of this microscopic gem.
description: Euastrum humerosum is a single-celled freshwater algae that belongs to a group called desmids - microscopic green algae known for their perfect symmetry and intricate beauty. This tiny organism is invisible to the naked eye, measuring only about 50-80 micrometers across (smaller than the width of a human hair). Each cell consists of two identical halves joined at the middle, creating a symmetrical shape that resembles a decorative star or ornate shield. You'll need a microscope to appreciate its geometric beauty and identify its characteristic features.

idTips.label: Symmetrical halves
idTips.description: The cell is perfectly divided into two identical mirror-image halves, like a folded paper cutout, with a clear constriction where they meet in the middle

idTips.label: Shoulder projections
idTips.description: Each half has distinctive shoulder-like bumps or projections that give the cell its characteristic broad, angular outline

idTips.label: Green coloration
idTips.description: The cell appears bright green under the microscope due to chloroplasts (the parts that photosynthesize), often with a slightly granular texture

idTips.label: Star-like outline
idTips.description: When viewed from above, the overall shape resembles a decorative star or ornate medallion with multiple points and indentations

idTips.label: Smooth cell wall
idTips.description: The outer edge appears relatively smooth and clean-cut, without the bumps, spines, or decorative patterns seen in some related species

habitat: You'll find Euastrum humerosum in clean, slightly acidic freshwater environments throughout New England, particularly in bog pools, pristine ponds, and slow-moving streams. It thrives in soft water with low mineral content, often in areas surrounded by sphagnum moss and other acid-loving plants. Look for it in undisturbed natural areas away from pollution, as desmids like this are sensitive to water quality changes.

seasonality.spring: Populations begin to grow as waters warm and daylight increases. This is often the best time to find them as they reproduce and become more numerous in the water column.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance occurs during warm months when photosynthesis is at its highest. Look for them in the upper layers of water where light penetration is best.
seasonality.fall: Numbers may decline as temperatures drop, but they can still be found. Some may form resistant stages to survive winter conditions.
seasonality.winter: Least active period, though they may persist in small numbers under ice. Some survive as dormant cells in sediments until spring returns.

funFact: Despite being a single cell, Euastrum humerosum is a master architect that can rebuild itself perfectly - when it reproduces, each half of the parent cell grows a brand new matching half, creating two identical offspring with the same intricate symmetrical pattern every single time, like a microscopic 3D printer that never makes mistakes!
confusionNotes: Euastrum humerosum can be confused with other desmid algae, especially fellow Euastrum species, but its distinctive shoulder projections and relatively smooth outline help distinguish it. Remember: if it looks like a symmetrical star with 'shoulders,' you've likely found your humerosum. Other desmids might be more circular, have spines, or lack the characteristic broad-shouldered appearance.
contextualKnowledge: Many people are surprised to learn that these microscopic algae are considered some of the most beautiful organisms on Earth by microscopists, with their perfect geometry rivaling any human-made art. Desmids like Euastrum were among the first organisms studied when microscopes were invented, and Victorian-era scientists often collected and arranged them like living jewels for display.
compareHints: Euastrum humerosum differs from its relatives by having more pronounced shoulder-like projections and a broader overall outline compared to species like E. bidentatum, which has a more tooth-like appearance. Unlike E. verrucosum, which has a warty or bumpy surface, E. humerosum maintains a relatively smooth cell wall. The shoulder projections are the key feature - they're more developed in humerosum than in most other New England Euastrum species.
